excerpt: Tables published in biomedical research papers, particularly supplemental tables, capture knowledge assertions that may not be in the main text of the manuscript for several reasons, including low statistical significance, space limitations, and narrative scope. These tables include data (e.g., association statistics, assay readouts, curated gene lists, and omics) encoding relationships between biological entities. Tablassert converts such tabular data (Excel, CSV, TSV, Parquet) into knowledge graphs ready for the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator (Fecho et al. 2025). A user declares in YAML how each table's data map to subject-predicate-object-qualifier statements; Tablassert resolves free text (e.g., ''lung cancer'') to standard identifiers, attaches provenance and statistics, and emits graph files conforming to Translator standards (D. Unni, Bruskiewich, and Moxon 2026; D. R. Unni et al. 2022).

title: Hybrid AI for AI-Native RAN Control: A Functional Perspective
author: Sabrine Aroua, Osama Arouk, Pegah Alizadeh
snippet: AI-native radio access network (RAN) control involves interdependent decisions across network entities, protocol layers, and timescales. Understanding how AI and conventional methods can jointly support these decisions requires a common basis for comparing their functional…
excerpt: AI-native radio access network (RAN) control involves interdependent decisions across network entities, protocol layers, and timescales. Understanding how AI and conventional methods can jointly support these decisions requires a common basis for comparing their functional roles. This survey introduces a technique-agnostic taxonomy of RAN decision-making organized around four complementary capabilities: Representation and Reasoning, Prediction and Simulation, Adaptive Control, and Decision Synthesis. These capabilities are defined by their roles in the control process, independently of the techniques used to implement them. Through this perspective, we examine representative AI and model-based approaches, including foundation models, world models, reinforcement learning, and optimization. We then apply the taxonomy to representative RAN control solutions across slow, medium, fast, and cross-timescale applications to identify which capabilities they implement and how these capabilities are combined in hybrid AI systems. We also review datasets, benchmarks, simulators, digital twins, and experimental platforms according to their support for the decision-making process and reproducible evaluation. The review highlights a gap between the availability of resources for closed-loop experimentation and the standardization of tasks, metrics, and evaluation protocols needed for meaningful comparisons.Finally, we identify research directions for hybrid AI in AI-native RAN, including capability integration, multi-agent and cross-timescale coordination, constraint handling, and reproducible closed-loop evaluation. A curated list of surveyed works and evaluation resources is available at

title: ArabFake: A multitask deep learning framework for Arabic fake news Detection, Categorization, and risk prediction
author: Ahmed Maher Khafaga Shehata, Mohammed Nasser Al-Suqri, Nour Eldin Mohamed Elshaiekh Osman, Faten Hamad, Yousuf Nasser Alhusaini, Ahmed Mahfouz
snippet: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary…
excerpt: The spread of fake news among Arabic media including social media represents a great challenge to the integrity of information and the trust of the public in it. In this paper, we introduce a comprehensive deep-learning framework, named ArabFake, that goes beyond the binary classification on Arabic fake news detection. ArabFake, built over MARBERTv2 (a state-of-the-art model for multi-dialectal Arabic tweets), proficiently address the complexity of the Arabic language while performing three unified tasks which are fake news detection, content categorization and its risk assessment. The framework promotes efficiency and performance both by enabling multi-task learning through shared knowledge representation across tasks. In order to facilitate development and evaluation, we present the ArabFake Dataset consisting of 2,495 manually labelled news items with labels that are verified by experts regarding fake news categories and risk levels. ArabFake demonstrates robust performance, achieving an F1 score of 94.12% for fake news detection, 84.92% for categorization, and 88.91% for risk zone assessment, highlighting its reliability and effectiveness across multiple tasks. We improve interpretability and extract insight into manipulative techniques by integrating valence scoring as part of the framework that emphasizes misleading linguistic cues used to disseminate fake news within the produced image. The results show that ArabFake is a holistic Arabic fake news detection framework that has practical implications on news organizations and fact checking projects.

title: fork() for Agents: Agent Kernel for Non-blocking LLM Orchestration
author: Ankit Chadha, Pratyay Banerjee
snippet: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and…
excerpt: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and recent agent runtimes (Sherlock, AgentGit, Atomix) preserve completed work through verifiers, version control, or transactional tool boundaries. We present \textbf{Agent-Kernel}, a non-blocking runtime that ports this pattern to the LLM \emph{content plane}: its primitive, \textbf{Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR)}, fires on a raw exception with no trained verifier or planner, resets a failed node's descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes each parent's text into its children's prompts (context inheritance), all on a durable substrate with a formal state-preservation guarantee. Across 14{,}434 runs on synthetic and standard benchmarks (tau-bench, Gaia2, AutomationBench, InterruptBench), SGR reaches full recovery within budget=3 where whole-trajectory replay exhausts (100\% vs.\ 55\%), and is roughly 10$\times$ faster than an adapted Sherlock rollback that also recovers. It matches ReAct-serial accuracy within noise on linear workloads while adding recovery and parallelism (up to 12.7$\times$ speedup) where structure permits. Ablation isolates SGR: removing it collapses success to 39.4\%.

title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
author: Tongxiao Hu, Yikai Zhao, Qiyan Zhao, Xiaosong Yuan, Xuhang Chen, Pengzhou Cheng, Xiaofeng Zhang
snippet: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired…
excerpt: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.

title: Generating Schema-Aligned Synthetic Dialogues and Measuring Their Diversity
author: Konrad Stolte, Toni Fetzer
snippet: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to…
excerpt: Training or evaluating a model that turns a conversation into a structured record requires paired data, meaning a transcript together with the exact record it should be converted into. Such pairs are expensive to annotate, and in sensitive domains they are also difficult to obtain at all. We therefore build them in the opposite order by sampling a schema-valid record first, then writing a dialogue from it, and optionally synthesizing speech from the dialogue, so the label exists before the text and we need no annotation step. Naively prompting a language model for such dialogues yields small variations of a single conversation, so we add a sampled variation configuration, personas, and a topic plan that orders the fields of the record as explicit mechanisms for variation. We measure the variation that reaches the output through embedding space, where the embedding variance spreads over about two and a half times as many independent directions with our full configuration compared to without (participation ratio 23.3 against 9.2). Two corpora of medical dialogue give values of the same order, with sample size, text length and language being additional factors there. We also show the positive effect of our method in a downstream test, where an 8B extraction model reaches 64.8% field accuracy when fine-tuned on dialogues from our method, against 57.5% from naive generation. We release the generation library and the generated corpus of German clinical dialogues with aligned records.

title: SkillCore: Internalizing Generalizable Skills via Scaffolding-Removed Fine-Tuning
author: Yi Liu, Changqing Ai, Peijie Dong, Xiankun Lin, Yongkang Yang, Zhezheng Hao, Xilin Xia, Hande Dong, Qiang Lin, Qiang Xu
snippet: Runtime skills can improve agents' problem-solving capabilities by providing procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging. However, these benefits reach only a minority of users, as most do not proactively invoke skills in practice. We argue that such…
excerpt: Runtime skills can improve agents' problem-solving capabilities by providing procedural guidance for tasks such as code review and debugging. However, these benefits reach only a minority of users, as most do not proactively invoke skills in practice. We argue that such generalizable procedures should become part of the model's capabilities rather than remain optional external add-ons, making them directly available without explicit skill loading. To this end, we present SkillCore, a data pipeline and supervised fine-tuning recipe for internalizing generalizable skills. We transform real agent trajectories by removing skill-loading scaffolding while preserving the task context and subsequent agent actions, thereby supervising direct execution without external skill content. To preserve access to task-specific skills that provide genuinely external information, we mix these scaffold-removed trajectories with a small proportion of skill-native trajectories that preserve supervision for skill invocation. On a held-out skill-free evaluation, SkillCore improves task completion quality over the base Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-72B models by 54.4% and 24.8%, respectively, while preserving task-specific skill invocation on a separate probe and general coding performance on SWE-bench Verified.

title: Sparse Poison, Strong Hijack: Efficient Trajectory-Level Backdoors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Only 1\% Poisoning
author: Simin Huang, Jiawei Chen, Shaolong Zhu, Qiwei Liang, Zhaoxia Yin
snippet: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than…
excerpt: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models advance robotic manipulation, but their reliance on demonstrations exposes them to backdoor threats. Among these threats, trajectory-level targeted backdoors are particularly challenging and may pose greater safety risks than behavior-disrupting attacks: rather than merely causing task failures or local action deviations, they must sustain closed-loop redirection to complete an attacker-specified multi-step task. To reliably induce such behaviors, existing methods typically rely on high poisoning rates to obtain sufficient target-trajectory supervision. However, high poisoning rates may compromise clean-task performance, whereas low rates leave target-trajectory supervision scarce and backdoor learning vulnerable to interference from dominant clean-task updates. To resolve this trade-off at low poisoning rates, we propose a two-stage co-optimization framework guided by vision, language, and action. Stage I freezes the policy and uses differentiable rendering and multimodal supervision to optimize a 3D trigger's texture, translation, and scale, strengthening trigger-target associations from limited poisoned demonstrations. Building on the optimized trigger, Stage II applies source-selective dual-LoRA adaptation to decouple clean and backdoor updates and mitigate their interference, followed by learned column-wise calibration and analytic fusion into a unified policy. Experiments on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_0$, and $\pi_{0.5}$ across four LIBERO suites show consistent gains over all evaluated attack baselines. With only 1% poisoned data, our method achieves 86.4% target success and 95.2% clean-task success on OpenVLA-OFT in LIBERO-Spatial. Real-robot trials also demonstrate trajectory-level hijacking.

title: Privacy Disclosure Control Benchmark (PDC-Bench): How Faithfully Do LLMs Keep Privacy Constraints on In-Context Disclosure Granularity?
author: Kosuke Fujita, Daiki Nishiyama, Jun Sakuma
snippet: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output…
excerpt: In LLM task execution, a constraint on the permitted disclosure granularity of personal attributes is sometimes imposed on the output. For example, if a person's private attribute is their location (San Francisco) and disclosure is permitted only at the country level, an output at the state level (California) violates the constraint. Detecting such violations requires capturing not only direct privacy leakage (San Francisco) but also semantic leakage (California). However, existing benchmarks cannot measure the degree of leakage with respect to a given semantic constraint such as the country-level limit. We therefore formalize disclosure control as a constraint on the permitted ceiling over the hierarchy of a knowledge graph. Building on this formulation, we construct PDC-Bench, a benchmark of 16,105 samples covering geography, age, race and ethnicity, and occupation. In our experiments applying PDC-Bench to eleven LLMs, 62% of the constraint violations were semantic leakage. We further found that semantic leakage depends less on the model than on the permitted disclosure granularity and the task's need for the private attribute; reliable auditing must therefore target semantic leakage together with these two factors. Data, prompts, and code are available at

title: RoboRecast: Intent-Preserving Demonstration Augmentation via Diagnosis-Driven Optimization
author: Yushi Long, Juzhan Xu, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Yin Chen, Sida Peng, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou
snippet: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior…
excerpt: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior that is semantically implausible or physically infeasible in the new setting. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. This flexibility allows RoboRecast to generate synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations and to adapt them to new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments. When target demonstrations are available, adding RoboRecast data improves policy success on both real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments.

title: Temporal Conditioning for Human Behavioral Cloning in Chess
author: Victor Dziwniel, Tianxiang Lu
snippet: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human…
excerpt: Behavioral cloning models in chess typically predict human moves from board states while ignoring temporal inputs such as the remaining clock. However, time pressure is a major determinant of human decision-making quality, and temporal state is a missing dimension of human behavioral modeling. This paper introduces a time-aware transformer that extends a Chessformer-style architecture with learned temporal conditioning tokens encoding player clock state, time control, and recent tempo, together with behavioral heads for thinking time and resignation. The model is trained on large-scale online chess data and evaluated against time-agnostic baselines and the state of the art. Results show that temporal conditioning yields modest overall accuracy improvements but substantially stronger gains under time pressure. Beyond move choice, it also produces more accurate thinking-time and resignation predictions. More importantly, the model better matches human move-quality degradation in critical time regimes, reducing the systematic over-strength observed in time-agnostic behavioral cloning models. These results suggest that temporal state is a previously underutilized but important signal for human behavioral cloning in chess.

title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
author: Frank T Wen, Kyler Rosen, Siddhi Ramesh, Michael Koo, Sara Kochanny, Sasha Jain-Liu, Emma Dyer, Alexander T Pearson, James M Dolezal
snippet: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved…
excerpt: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV (95% CI 59.0-73.9%), 69.3% for MSI (95% CI 51.9-76.5%) and 63.4%-81.2% for breast signatures. Cross-scanner prostate grade agreement rose from 42.5% to 92.7%. Under full scanner-HPV confounding during training, AUROC fell from 0.80 to 0.68 with original model features but only from 0.86 to 0.84 with tempering. Unlike post hoc feature calibration, tempering used only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site calibration. These findings support tempering to reduce scanner dependence of pathology foundation models.

title: GRUN: Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network for Image Restoration
author: Rihan Zhang, Fengyang Xiao, Yuhan Chen, Chunming He, Sina Farsiu
snippet: Image restoration remains a fundamental challenge in low-level vision, requiring methods that handle diverse degradations while preserving scene structures and details. We revisit classical Retinex theory and propose a Generalized Retinex formulation that extends the…
excerpt: Image restoration remains a fundamental challenge in low-level vision, requiring methods that handle diverse degradations while preserving scene structures and details. We revisit classical Retinex theory and propose a Generalized Retinex formulation that extends the illumination-reflectance decomposition into a Retinex-inspired content-environment factorization prior for image restoration. The key idea is to restore images using two learned factors: a content-dominant response (generalized reflectance) capturing scene properties and an environment-side response (generalized illumination) encoding task-dependent variations associated with the observed degradations. Based on this formulation, we develop GRUN (Generalized Retinex Unfolding Network), a MAP-guided deep unfolding framework that alternates reflectance restoration, illumination estimation, and progressive degradation inference across K stages with degradation-conditioned proximal operators. We further introduce a Degradation-aware Coupling Regularizer (DCR) that combines mutual information minimization, gradient decorrelation, and scale anchoring to promote complementary content-environment factor representations. Experiments on seven image restoration tasks, including denoising, dehazing, deraining, low-light enhancement, deblurring, underwater enhancement, and backlit enhancement, demonstrate competitive results on multiple benchmarks using the same architecture with task-specific weights. Moreover, the proposed Generalized Retinex design can be integrated into existing restoration methods, demonstrating its cross-architecture applicability. Code will be released.

title: Next-Manip: On-Demand Agent-Policy Collaboration for Robotic Manipulation
author: Jiayi Liu, Ke Ye, Jiaming Zhou, Yufei Huang, Haotian Liang, Kun-Yu Lin, Junwei Liang
snippet: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack…
excerpt: General-purpose robotic manipulation requires task reasoning, failure recovery, and precise control, yet limited manipulation data make these abilities difficult to obtain from a single policy. Recent multimodal agents show promise in task reasoning and recovery but lack reliable fine-grained control and incur high inference cost, whereas learned policies provide efficient fine-grained execution but struggle beyond their learned skills. Although their complementary strengths suggest combining the two, doing so requires repeatedly deciding which executor should act as task demands change. Instead of relying on the agent for each decision, we present Next-Manip, an on-demand agent--policy collaboration framework that decouples executor allocation from costly agent inference. We propose an Agent Invocation Controller (AIC) that allocates control between the policy and the agent through a lightweight classifier of current execution demands. We further introduce Task Dynamics Context (TDC), which packages informative manipulation changes from in-context examples into compact task references to support both agent reasoning and executor allocation. Across two simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments, Next-Manip achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing agent inference costs.

title: EviCraft: Can Minecraft Agents Find What They Cannot See?
author: Wenyou Yi, Lantian Zhang, Guanlin Chen, Xingqiu Xu, Haiyang Sun, Minrui Huang, Tianle Liang, Hao Chen, Haorui Xu, Zhou Zhao
snippet: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We…
excerpt: In Minecraft, a common testbed for embodied agents, semantic tools such as mineBlock pick targets from the simulator's loaded world state without a visibility test, so a buried ore the agent has never seen is one call away, and scores cannot show whether the agent searched. We formalize the missing requirement as evidence closure: every decision of an agent system, including those inside its tools, may depend on the world only through facts for which the agent holds evidence. EviCraft is a runtime and benchmark that enforces closure below the agent and makes the admission rule an experimental variable: a perception-grounded regime (G) admits only what is in line of sight or returned by the agent's own actions, and a loaded-state regime (L) reproduces standard tool stacks, with agents, tools, and worlds held fixed. On Survival, the regime effect exceeds the strongest agent's lead: under G, three mid-sized agents reach the diamond in 32%-40% of runs, against 76%-94% under L, and the strongest agent under G scores below each of them under L. In two models, removing only the line-of-sight test closes 93%-96% of the score gap, and loading state only inside tools recovers 70%-98%, so safeguards on observations and queries leave most of the leak open. In open-ended acquisition, the gain from L concentrates in items that depend on buried resources or mobs. Code and benchmark are available at

title: Beyond Before-and-After Images: Evaluating Temporal Grounding in a Lightweight VLM for Disaster Assessment
author: Shubh Garg, Pratham Arora, Debabrata Ghosh
snippet: Bi-temporal satellite imagery is central to disaster assessment: deciding what was damaged requires comparing a pre-event scene with its post-event counterpart. A vision-language model (VLM) can nonetheless appear to answer change questions while relying mainly on the…
excerpt: Bi-temporal satellite imagery is central to disaster assessment: deciding what was damaged requires comparing a pre-event scene with its post-event counterpart. A vision-language model (VLM) can nonetheless appear to answer change questions while relying mainly on the post-event image or on the prompt's temporal framing. We present a controlled diagnostic of temporal grounding and apply it to one lightweight VLM, InternVL3-2B, on DisasterM3: 1,659 optical and SAR image pairs from 41 events and nine disaster types, in event-disjoint partitions, with 9,031 reasoning questions. We compare post-only input, the true pre/post pair, the post image repeated twice, reversed image order, and an unrelated pre-event image. The true pair scores $+0.5$ accuracy points above the repeated-post control (95\% paired bootstrap CI $[-0.2, +1.2]$), and reversing the order changes accuracy by $-0.2$ points ($[-0.8, +0.5]$). Under this protocol we therefore find no measurable benefit from the content of the true pre-event image and little sensitivity to temporal order. The model is not blind to the first image, however: the true pair scores $2.5$ points above a pair whose pre-event image comes from another event ($[+1.6, +3.4]$). State-transition and multi-hop questions remain hard, and optical and SAR inputs show different profiles. We outline temporal scene graphs as a testable next step, not a validated solution, and argue that temporal benchmarks for Earth observation should report whether answers depend on the intended evidence, not only how often they are right.

title: Your VLM Knows What to Inspect: Semantic Probe-Guided Adaptive Focusing for GUI Grounding
author: Ruixiao Shi, Fu Feng, Yucheng Xie, Jing Wang, Xin Geng
snippet: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models…
excerpt: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.

title: BEACON: Learning Observation-Conditioned Starting Points for Guided Conditional Flow Matching in Microscopy
author: Anirban Ray, Florian Jug
snippet: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling…
excerpt: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Computational restoration can recover high-quality images from such data, enabling cheaper and faster imaging at lower light dose, provided biologically meaningful structures are preserved. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. However, it pairs each clean target with an independent standard Gaussian sample, so the starting point of every training path does not leverage the degraded observation. This arbitrary noise--target coupling can produce conflicting velocity targets and makes the conditional velocity field harder to learn. We present BEACON, a $BE$st-of-$K$ $A$daptive learned coupling for guided $CON$ditional flow matching, which learns an observation-conditioned base distribution. During training, a lightweight conditional noise model proposes $K$ starting points for each degraded input, and the candidate with the lowest flow-matching loss supervises both networks, while a KL term keeps the proposal close to the Gaussian prior. At inference, a single draw from the learned proposal is transported along the velocity field, requiring neither candidate selection nor the target. We evaluate BEACON on ten datasets spanning microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution against 13 baseline families. BEACON achieves the best median perception--distortion rank for every pairing of a fidelity metric (PSNR, MicroMS-SSIM) with a perceptual metric (LPIPS, FID). Code and pretrained models will be released under a permissive license.

title: GreenDynaMix: Thermal-Aware Dynamic Mixed-Precision MoE LLM Inference Systems
author: Han-Yi Lin, Kieran Griperay, Qiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhou, Nate Bonacci, Zinachidi Achikeh, Li He, Shaofei Qi, Hongqiang Wang, Jeff Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Pi-Cheng Hsiu, Jingtong Hu
snippet: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time…
excerpt: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.

title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
author: Jiaming Liu, Fenlou Zhai, Ao Xue, Liangliang Tang, Cheng Ding, Daoqiang Zhang
snippet: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope…
excerpt: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. Pressure-based monitoring must accommodate flow responses that vary with operating condition and measurement location. InletScope combines shared multiscale pressure encoding, learned scale fusion and sensor-probability averaging, allowing measurement sets to change without retraining. Separate models evaluate unstart detection and new-onset prediction within a 0.5-s future interval. Seven Mach-2.9 runs, each with one annotated event, cover downstream throttling, throat regulation and splitter adjustment; three are held out with fixed weights and source-derived settings. Across three training seeds, full-sensor detection achieves run-wise mean window $F_1$ scores of 0.834--0.964. Eight-sensor aggregation reduces detection-score variation across sensor subsets in both splitter runs while retaining mean scores close to those of the full sets. Regional detection favors cowl and high-speed-channel measurements during splitter adjustment and compression-side measurements during downstream throttling, consistent with their respective pressure responses. Complete-record evaluation shows that configurations with comparable window scores can produce different alarm timing and persistence. These findings connect sensor count and regional coverage to pressure discrimination and sequential alarm behavior, providing experimental guidance for configuring inlet monitoring systems.

title: Calm Agent: Reframing Agent Interaction around Intermittent Human Attention
author: Dian Jin, Zixun Fu, Guan Wang, Yancheng Yuan
snippet: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention…
excerpt: AI agents can carry out auxiliary tasks while users focus on other work. Yet users still need to understand task state, make changes, and respond when help is required. We argue that agents for ongoing auxiliary tasks should be designed around intermittent human attention: tasks should continue between interactions, and users should be able to return with little effort to understand and control them. We develop this position as Calm Agent. It connects three on-demand interaction modes: Delegate, Adjust, and Check, through a persistent task representation. Generative interaction provides controls and feedback suited to open-ended goals, while existing controls support routine actions. We illustrate these principles with Orvlet, a desktop prototype for background execution and compact task interfaces. We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

title: No Fixed Configuration Is Best: Context- and Cost-Aware Tuning of LLM Pipelines, with an Application to Schema Matching and Mapping
author: Gokhan Kirlik, Xiuwen Zheng, Anirudh Sriram
snippet: The numeric settings of a multi-stage LLM pipeline (a compound AI system) are the usual target of tuning. We tuned all of them for an LLM pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, and we show what this buys, what it cannot buy, and…
excerpt: The numeric settings of a multi-stage LLM pipeline (a compound AI system) are the usual target of tuning. We tuned all of them for an LLM pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, and we show what this buys, what it cannot buy, and where the remaining accuracy is. First, tuning buys cost and a little accuracy. On 35 tasks, with whole groups of tasks held out from tuning, one tuned configuration gains 2.9 points of top-1 accuracy (HR@1) over the default at 18% more cost, and another keeps the accuracy of the default at 32% lower cost. Second, the accuracy depends on a choice that numeric tuning cannot reach. Restricting the search for each source column to one assigned target table changes HR@1 by +30 points on a MIMIC-III to OMOP task and by -52 points on a task built from database views, more than numeric tuning gains on nine of ten test tasks. Neither setting is right for all tasks: on the larger set of 41 tasks used for the remaining results, mean HR@1 is 75.7% with the restriction (the default) and 83.1% without it. Third, choosing the setting per task is not enough either: even an oracle that picks the better setting for each task reaches only 87.8% on the 41 tasks, because the better setting differs between the columns of one task. The pipeline therefore runs both settings, and an LLM judge chooses among their candidate answers on the 26% of columns on which they disagree. This reaches 91.5% HR@1 on the 41 tasks, at 5.9 times the cost of the default, about one cent per column.

title: SALSA: Sampling Adversarial Suffixes from Learned Distributions for LLM Safety Assessment
author: Shivank Rajput, Himanshu Singh, A. V. Subramanyam
snippet: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference…
excerpt: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where adversaries append optimized suffixes to otherwise benign looking prompts to bypass safety alignment. Existing optimization-based GCG-style attacks can be effective, but they are expensive at inference time, and suffer from poor transfer. We present, SALSA, a generative framework that learns a distribution over jailbreak suffixes from optimization-derived attack corpora. Once trained, the model supports efficient sampling-based attacks. On open-source targets, it achieves attack success rates comparable to state-of-the-art optimization baselines, while reducing generation time from 3.46s to 0.04s per prompt. In black-box transfer, it remains highly effective against proprietary systems, including 99% ASR on GPT-3.5-Turbo, and reaches 45% ASR on the substantially harder GPT-4o, more than doubling the strongest baseline at an equal sampling budget. We further offer an intuition for why generative sampling can preserve high attack success, when the learned suffix distribution is close to the distribution of optimization outputs. Overall, our results show that learning adversarial suffix distributions yields a scalable, and practically efficient foundation for continuous LLM vulnerability discovery.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Candidate Generation for Entity Linking in Cyber Threat Intelligence
author: Nasser Alkhulaifi, Direnc Pekaslan, Christian Wagner
snippet: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the…
excerpt: Entity Resolution (ER) pipelines often collapse ambiguity into early hard decisions: upstream Named Entity Recognition (NER) selects a single span and type, and downstream Entity Linking (EL) treats that choice as ground truth. This discards valuable information about the ambiguity of the underlying data (e.g., span boundary disagreement and type confusion), leading to brittle systems that fail unpredictably when faced with uncertainty in inputs. Therefore, this work presents a proof-of-concept for uncertainty-aware ER that treats uncertainty as native data that should be preserved and exploited throughout ER pipelines. We (i) capture uncertainty signals in the NER stage and (ii) leverage these signals into the EL stage to improve candidate retrieval under ambiguity. Using a BERT-based NER model augmented with two auxiliary span-boundary prediction heads, we apply Monte Carlo (MC) dropout at inference time to derive three mention-level proxy signals: the MC-averaged start-boundary probability, the MC-averaged end-boundary probability, and De Luca-Termini fuzzy entropy computed over the Begin-Inside-Outside (BIO) predictive distribution. These signals are used to adapt the fuzzy cutoff in candidate generation (CG) for EL. Because CG is treated as a blocking step, we evaluate retrieval recall. On the AnnoCTR dataset linked to the MITRE ATTCK knowledge base, the boundary-aware and dual-signal fuzzy linking approaches improve Recall@10 from 0.6186 to 0.7966. The contribution lies not in an end-to-end optimised ER pipeline but in establishing uncertainty preservation as a viable and beneficial component of ER pipelines, enabling downstream EL to make better-informed decisions under uncertainty.

title: Machine learning enables full Bayesian inference for spinning extreme-mass-ratio inspirals
author: Bo Liang, Minghui Du, Zhenwei Lyu, Hanlin Song, Jiakai Zhang, Weichen Qin, Chia-Jui Chou, Yi Yang, Jingyi Yu, Ziren Luo, Mingming Sun, Peng Xu, Yue-Liang Wu
snippet: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar-mass compact objects spiralling into massive black holes, promise to measure the masses and spins of the central black holes, reveal the strong-field environment around them and gauge cosmic distances via millihertz…
excerpt: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar-mass compact objects spiralling into massive black holes, promise to measure the masses and spins of the central black holes, reveal the strong-field environment around them and gauge cosmic distances via millihertz gravitational-wave observations. Yet most forecasts for the parameter inference of these systems assume known source parameters, and broad-prior analyses have addressed only simplified versions of the problem. The joint inversion of all 14 parameters of a spinning source from the complete prior has remained unsolved. Here we solve it for the augmented analytic kludge model: generative networks narrow the complete prior and reveal a ring of degenerate spin directions, and the exact detector likelihood determines the posterior. For a simulated one-year LISA-Taiji observation, within one ring sector we obtain, for the first time, a 14-parameter posterior of a spinning EMRI from the complete prior, the most precise yet obtained for such a source from broad priors. The redshifted mass and spin of the massive black hole are determined to two parts in $10^5$, the mass two orders of magnitude beyond any electromagnetic measurement. The compact object's redshifted mass is measured to one part in $10^4$, and its eccentric, retrograde orbit discriminates between capture channels. The 0.8% distance and sub-square-degree localization are sufficient for dark-siren cosmology. Year-long coherent analysis resolves the inspiral driven by radiation reaction itself.

title: VC-OPD: Learning to See What Matters via Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation
author: Qinxuan Wang, Zheyu Zhang, Yijing Yang, Han Shu, Chuang Wang, Peipei Yang, Shuo Tang, Jie Hu, Shiming Xiang
snippet: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual…
excerpt: Visual On-Policy Distillation (OPD) commonly uses cropped or zoomed-in image regions as teacher-side privileged information to improve fine-grained perception in small Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). However, local pixel-level cues are insufficient for complex visual reasoning that requires global structure, spatial relationships, and high-level semantics. We propose Visual Cue On-Policy Self-Distillation (VC-OPD), which extends teacher-side privileged information beyond local image regions to question-conditioned visual cues. Advanced MLLMs generate cues capturing key visual details, structural relationships, and semantic evidence needed to answer each question. A multi-stage quality filtering process selects reliable cues, which are provided only to the teacher during training. This enables informative token-level supervision along student-generated trajectories, helping the student learn to identify and reason over critical evidence directly from the original image. No additional information is required at inference time. Since advanced MLLMs are used only for visual cue generation, VC-OPD is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary black-box models. Experiments on STEM and general visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements across model scales over reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation baselines. Notably, a 4B model trained with VC-OPD outperforms many baselines with 8B or more parameters, demonstrating effective capability transfer through question-conditioned visual cues.

title: Lexical Tone and Word Order Matter in Translation: Prosodic Correspondence Across Languages
author: Haopeng Xie, Ismail Rasim Ulgen, Shengying Zhao, Berrak Sisman, Philipp Koehn
snippet: Prosody conveys emphasis, emotion, and intent, yet its correspondence across translation remains underexplored, especially when languages differ in lexical tone and word order. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic word-level analysis of prosodic correspondence in…
excerpt: Prosody conveys emphasis, emotion, and intent, yet its correspondence across translation remains underexplored, especially when languages differ in lexical tone and word order. To our knowledge, we present the first systematic word-level analysis of prosodic correspondence in translated speech spanning tonal and non-tonal Asian languages, with comparisons to European-language findings and explicit analyses of lexical tone and word reordering. Building on prior evidence of fine-grained prosody correspondence in European-language pairs, we investigate how these linguistic factors relate to word-level pitch and energy correspondence between English and five languages: Mandarin Chinese, Thai, and Vietnamese, which have lexical tone, and Japanese and Korean as additional comparisons. Correspondence is generally lower than previously reported European-language estimates. Adjusting for lexical tone increases pitch correspondence for English-Mandarin Chinese, English-Thai, and English-Vietnamese. However, English-Japanese and English-Korean also exhibit lower correspondence than the European-language estimates, indicating that tonal status alone does not explain the observed pattern. Greater word reordering is associated with weaker local correspondence even under semantic alignment, suggesting that semantic alignment does not fully account for differences in prosodic organization. These findings characterize the limits of fine-grained acoustic correspondence across translation and motivate prosody modeling that accounts for lexical pitch constraints and the structural context of translated content.

title: From Memory Access to Evidence Sufficiency: Diagnosing and Addressing Demand--Evidence Misalignment
author: Shiyao Liu, Yixing Fan, Ruqing Zhang, Xiaohui Yan, Jiafeng Guo, Xueqi Cheng
snippet: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence…
excerpt: Long-term memory retrieval often returns query-relevant records, but relevance does not guarantee sufficient evidence: answering requires a set of records that jointly satisfies a question's factual, relational, temporal, and state constraints. We study this demand--evidence misalignment through MemPath, an interventional framework that diagnoses failures in memory access, demand coverage, and evidence utilization. Guided by this diagnosis, we propose BiDE-Mem, which represents questions as typed demands and uses them to guide retrieval and evidence organization. We formalize demand--evidence support; in the evaluated compact path, it is conveyed through provenance-aware evidence organization and Reader guidance rather than a separate generative four-state verification step. On LoCoMo, BiDE-Mem improves accuracy by 6.23 percentage points over Mnemis; on LongMemEval, it achieves 91.80%, with strong multi-hop and temporal performance. Supplementary Qwen-Reader evaluations place it first among seven systems on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S under two judging protocols. Ablations and evidence-level analyses show that demand representation, retrieval, and evidence presentation each contribute to answer quality.

title: GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures
author: Qian Chen, Kun Zhu, Zhongyi Wang, Ling Chen
snippet: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of…
excerpt: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
author: Yuisei Iwata, Yutaka Masuda, Tohru Ishihara
snippet: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further…
excerpt: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
author: Hongjia Liu, Dacheng Zhou, Minghao Fu, Chuanjun Guo, Tianze Wang, Qingtao Liu, He Wang, Li Yi
snippet: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions…
excerpt: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $\pi_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.

title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
author: Jiewen Hou, Guanxiang Qi, Meina Kan, Shiguang Shan, Xilin Chen
snippet: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of…
excerpt: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.

title: Reproducing the Speech Labels of Qwen3-Omni's Talker: Mimi in bf16, and a Last-Frame Pitfall
author: Yuxuan Chen
snippet: Qwen3-Omni speaks through a Talker predicting 16 codebooks of a 12.5 Hz audio codec, but the encoder that made its training labels was not released, so new voices cannot be trained on matching labels. We identify this encoder from the released model's behavior. White-box…
excerpt: Qwen3-Omni speaks through a Talker predicting 16 codebooks of a 12.5 Hz audio codec, but the encoder that made its training labels was not released, so new voices cannot be trained on matching labels. We identify this encoder from the released model's behavior. White-box regression shows that the codebook embeddings of the Talker, its multi-token predictor and the Code2Wav decoder match the first 16 codebooks of kyutai's Mimi layer by layer. A decoder-based test looks convincing but fails calibration: decoders trained on known labels cannot tell them apart. Teacher-forced Talker likelihoods, calibrated with 13 code language models trained on known labels, do tell implementations apart: the Talker prefers labels from kyutai's moshi package with bf16 weights over every other variant we tried. Loudness normalization and band-limiting of 20% or more of the data are ruled out. Separately, transformers' MimiModel encodes the last frame differently from kyutai's encoder unless the input length is a multiple of 1920 samples. After LoRA fine-tuning on its labels, 44--55% of generated sentences end in a noise burst, and the same frame costs the Mimi-based CSM-1B 119 nats; padding the input removes both. We release the encoding recipe, a label checker and a Talker fine-tuning toolkit.

title: The algorithmic behavioral sink: Modeling the transition to irreversible demographic collapse
author: Feng Yu
snippet: In 2025, the vast majority of major global economies reported a Total Fertility Rate below the replacement level of 2.1. This synchronized collapse has persisted despite extensive pro-natalist financial interventions, revealing a structural limitation in conventional linear…
excerpt: In 2025, the vast majority of major global economies reported a Total Fertility Rate below the replacement level of 2.1. This synchronized collapse has persisted despite extensive pro-natalist financial interventions, revealing a structural limitation in conventional linear demographic models. This paper proposes that the ubiquity of mobile internet and Artificial Intelligence acts as a synthetic mating disruptor, precipitating a non-linear phase transition in human pair-bonding dynamics. Treating the marriage market as a complex system governed by thermodynamic constraints, we present a Fermi-Dirac selection model, using national income distributions as the input spectrum and fitted with Japanese longitudinal data to illustrate how digital hyper-reality generates an increasingly prohibitive Marriage Energy Barrier. Our model quantifies a Tech Factor that decouples female mating expectations from local economic realities during initial courtship, a distortion we predict will be severely exacerbated as AI evolves into an emotional substitute. Projections indicate that this substitution effect is accelerating; without intervention, the world post 2040 risks entering an irreversible demographic contraction, as the sudden surge in TFR required for recovery is biologically impossible. Ultimately, this framework explains why traditional financial subsidies fail to reverse falling birth rates and suggests that digital convenience may represent a behavioral Great Filter that erodes the imperative for species persistence.

title: Agentic Optimization: LLM Agents Select and Configure Algorithms for Engineering Design
author: Dominic Mashak, Jacob Schrum
snippet: Engineers solving new multi-objective design problems commonly commit to a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) before seeing a result. The best MOEA differs from benchmark to benchmark. We propose agentic optimization, placing an LLM agent outside the optimization…
excerpt: Engineers solving new multi-objective design problems commonly commit to a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) before seeing a result. The best MOEA differs from benchmark to benchmark. We propose agentic optimization, placing an LLM agent outside the optimization loop, where it reads a natural-language problem description to configure and launch algorithms, drawing on parametric knowledge rather than on a performance history that a novel problem lacks. We compare five LLMs in a fixed harness on four engineering benchmarks and a real-world SARS-CoV-2 molecular docking task, using hypervolume (HV) and IGD+ with multiple comparison-corrected tests. Three models (GPT, DeepSeek, Qwen) dominate every baseline on combined HV and IGD+, and each is significantly better than the best baseline on at least one benchmark, sometimes by applying the same baseline algorithm they surpass, showing the importance of both algorithm configuration and selection. Agent behavior is strongly model-dependent, but even the weakest agents dominate three of the four baselines overall.

title: Fresh Keys, Stale Secrets: Numeric Leakage across Linked LLM Prompts
author: Jian Li, Qinglin Zhao, Shuoyao Wang, Jincheng Cai, Zhifeng Hao, Naiqi Wu
snippet: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new…
excerpt: Small businesses repeatedly ask cloud language models about the same confidential prices, unit costs and margins. Numeric prompt disguises for such numbers are evaluated one prompt at a time, but a provider sees a firm's history, in which each fresh secret gives a new, independent view of the same numbers. Since real costs are not public, we measure on synthetic firms with known values how much an honest-but-curious provider recovers when it knows the disguise algorithm, holds sector-level price and margin statistics, and links a firm's queries. In one prompt, per-field scaling, a fixed-axis instantiation of Zhang et al.'s order-preserving substitution and Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt's released sanitizer keep the attacker's margin-hit advantage over a prior-only guess between -0.6 and +4.4 percentage points. After 16 linked queries with fresh secrets, every disguise we test (Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon\geq 0.5$) has a target recovered significantly more often: under the order-preserving substitution, margin recovery rises from 25.0% to 59.4%. The same attacker recovers 29.4 percentage points more margins with fresh maps than with one reused map. Theory explains the contrast: one reused secret bounds all queries by a single full-precision view of the fields shown, whereas fresh scaling keys are identifiable. Except for Pr$\varepsilon\varepsilon$mpt at $\varepsilon=0.5$, the gains persist when the attacker's prior comes from another population model and when values drift by up to 5% between queries; on our firms, whose prose cues are weak, reading the prose with a language model adds at most 2.5 points. title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
author: Kaushal Mhapsekar, Darsh Asher, Bita Aslrousta, Amna Hassan, Debayan Sengupta, Azam Ghanbari, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz
snippet: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound…
excerpt: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j
author: Rajat M. Barot, Arjun S. Borkhatariya
snippet: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j…
excerpt: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete CircuitBreaker/Retry/Bulkhead configurations from Prometheus signals. Our first, naive design scored worse than keeping the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios under the reward it optimised: exploring a menu that contained aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic while the learner was still learning. Two safeguards fix this: a safe policy menu (no breaker stricter than the latency SLO) and safe exploration with a bounded reward. With them, AdaptR4j beats the production default in every winnable scenario (p < 0.001, three runs each, run-to-run SD <= 0.03), beats the best fixed policy when the fault changes over time, and cuts user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared with the naive design. A context-free bandit on the same safe menu performs statistically indistinguishably, so the safeguards - not the learner - carry most of the benefit. We also report how an earlier version of our harness produced convincing but wrong results: a unit mismatch made every circuit breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.

title: A Generative AI Agent to Emulate Interactive Human-driven Vehicles for Automated Driving Testing in Urban Areas
author: Jia Hu, Changjian Yu, Panqu Wang, Jaehyun So, Yang Chang, Xuerun Yan, Jintao Lai
snippet: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical interactions involving high collision risk for the following reasons: they often…
excerpt: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical interactions involving high collision risk for the following reasons: they often assume full observability, overlooking interactions arising from occlusion. Driving styles are mainly characterized by vehicle maneuvers, limiting the diversity of safety-critical interaction behaviors. Moreover, learning signals from safety-critical interactions can be diluted by non-critical driving behaviors. To address these issues, we propose a generative AI agent to emulate interactive HDVs. The agent incorporates field-of-view modeling to account for driver visibility under occlusion and characterizes the interaction process using five metrics spanning its initial, intermediate, and final stages. It automatically learns diverse interaction styles through a dynamic mixture-of-experts network. Through residual reinforcement learning, the agent further refines generated trajectories to match the real-world distributions of safety-critical interaction characteristics. Experiments on the INTERACTION dataset show that our method reduces Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) by 39.9\%--87.1\% across five interaction characteristics compared with a state-of-the-art baseline. Our method achieves greater improvements of up to 87.1\% in final-stage interaction metrics, suggesting that it can reduce error accumulation in long-horizon trajectory generation. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component, particularly highlighting the importance of residual refinement. Generalization experiments show that our method approaches the performance of full training on unseen intersections with only one epoch of fine-tuning.

title: Interactive Neural Computers
author: Ross Murphy, Marcel Hedman, Gabriel Brostow
snippet: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We…
excerpt: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

title: BRAG: Bayesian Retrieval Augmented Generation
author: Javier Movellan, Manjot Bilkhu, Young-mok Jung, Sirajul Salekin, Henry Tran, Zhao Huang
snippet: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a…
excerpt: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also shows when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.

title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
author: Binfei Ji, Zhiwen Cao, Anqi Yang, Prem Seetharaman, Shuo Yang, Ratheesh Kalarot, Yingyan Celine Lin, Mingze Xu
snippet: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled…
excerpt: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.

title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
author: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
